source.title: On the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Textbooks Need an Update

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full thesis, including its empirical chapter and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The thesis directly measures bias and variance as fully connected networks widen and reports test-error trends, refining the claim that wider networks must incur higher variance. Its test-error results also bear on V2.
record.gate_note: The central width experiments report qualitative bias, variance, and test-error trends. No exact test-error values are given in the text; graph values are not reconstructed. Cited results from other studies, including Neyshabur et al. (2015), are excluded.
record.test_reason: The thesis reports its own width-versus-test-error experiments in single-hidden-layer fully connected networks trained without explicit regularization, directly bearing on V2. Its refutation of a universal bias–variance tradeoff concerns a different claim and does not justify T5 for V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the empirical conclusion: bias and variance can decrease together as networks widen; optimization-related variance decreases, while sampling-related variance increases slowly and plateaus. The thesis additionally argues that textbooks should qualify the universality of the bias–variance tradeoff.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies width and measures test error, but its main contribution directly measures bias and variance. It uses fully connected networks on several tasks, with details differing from the specific model and data conditions stated in V2.
record.method_sensitivity: For small MNIST, the decreasing-bias trend depends on tuning step size by network size; with a fixed step size of 0.01, bias does not decrease monotonically. The reported qualitative variance trend also appears with batch gradient descent and LBFGS on small MNIST. Varying depth gives different outcomes: variance slowly increases with dynamical isometry and test error degrades for vanilla and skip-connected networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction bias and variance can decrease together with width; optimization variance falls while sampling variance increases slowly and plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing neural-network width need not create a tradeoff between prediction bias and prediction variance.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider networks learn increasingly similar functions on a noisy sinusoid regression task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width can reduce prediction variability in noisy sinusoid regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing depth worsens test error in vanilla and skip-connected networks; dynamical isometry yields only about a 0.1 percentage-point increase from depth 25 to 200.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization under increasing depth depends on architecture and training conditions.

record.problems: The text gives qualitative descriptions for several test-error trends whose values are shown only in figures. The small-data MNIST result depends on step-size tuning by network size. The authors note that they do not study how bias and variance change over the course of training. Theoretical arguments rely on strong assumptions.

untested.parts: No original comparison of fixed random-label memorization with natural-label held-out generalization.
ReLU activations and downsampled CIFAR-10 are not established. The precise width at zero training error and the interpolation-threshold test-error peak are not established by the readable results.
No controlled batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps.
No memorized-example removal and retraining experiment.

missing.what: Small-MNIST width experiment with fixed learning rate 0.01, including the explicitly described U-shaped error curve and corresponding training errors. Add a condition-specific row; the exact post-interpolation segment requires the figure.
CIFAR-10 width-versus-test-error results with early stopping, a separate training condition from R2. The supplied text preserves the caption but not readable curves.

Small-MNIST test-error results with full-batch gradient descent and LBFGS. These figures contain relevant optimizer-specific width comparisons; decreasing variance alone cannot determine their test-error verdicts.
missing.locator: Appendix B.6, Figures B.8 and B.9

record.verdict_notes: Unreadable figure curves are evidence limitations, not limits_scope findings. Accordingly, R2 and R3 do not justify the record's limits_scope label. No listed original source matches this thesis.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.

The experiments use fully connected networks, but activation details are not stated. The text does not establish that these are the specific one-hidden-layer ReLU networks or downsampled CIFAR-10 setting named in the version. It does not test the interpolation-threshold peak or double descent.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance is not compared.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization is not compared.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the generalization gap are not measured.

relationships.display_finding: Test error decreased as width increased, with networks generally trained beyond perfect training accuracy but no width-specific interpolation thresholds established.

relationships.reason: Based on Appendix B.5 text, missing from the rows: the authors explicitly describe a U-shaped curve and attribute it to width-dependent learning-rate suitability; improvement with width therefore depends on this recipe choice.
relationships.display_finding: The reported reversal, attributed to how suitable the learning rate was at different widths, remains unverified. The exact range of widths beyond interpolation where performance worsened remains unresolved.
